title: What is the Catalyst Optimizer and how does it work (Parsed Logical Plan → Analyzed → Optimized Logical Plan with predicate pushdown/column pruning → Physical Plan with WholeStageCodegen)?
topicTitle: What is the Catalyst Optimizer and how does it work

s1_definition.profdef: The Catalyst Optimizer is Spark SQL's extensible query optimizer that transforms a DataFrame or SQL query into an efficient execution plan through a series of phases. It builds a parsed logical plan from the query, analyzes it by resolving column and table names against the catalog, rewrites it into an optimized logical plan using rule-based optimizations like predicate pushdown and column pruning, and then produces one or more physical plans, selecting the cheapest and often compiling operators into tight JVM bytecode through whole-stage code generation.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India is handed a sloppy request: "bring me every single transaction record for the whole bank, then I'll pick out Rajesh's, then I'll look only at the amount column." Catalyst is the smart supervisor who rewrites that request before anyone moves: "only fetch Rajesh's records, and only the amount column." The supervisor first checks the request makes sense and the columns exist, then applies known efficiency rules, then decides the fastest physical way to do it, and even hands the clerk a pre-printed streamlined worksheet instead of loose instructions. The result arrives far faster, and the person who wrote the request did not have to think about any of it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Catalyst turns a DataFrame or SQL query into an efficient plan through parse, analyze, optimize, and physical planning, cutting data read via predicate pushdown and column pruning and speeding execution with whole-stage code generation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Catalyst Optimizer is Spark SQL's extensible query optimizer that transforms a DataFrame or SQL query into an efficient execution plan through a series of phases. It builds a parsed logical plan from the query, analyzes it by resolving column and table names against the catalog, rewrites it into an optimized logical plan using rule-based optimizations like predicate pushdown and column pruning, and then produces one or more physical plans, selecting the cheapest and often compiling operators into tight JVM bytecode through whole-stage code generation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India is handed a sloppy request: "bring me every single transaction record for the whole bank, then I'll pick out Rajesh's, then I'll look only at the amount column." Catalyst is the smart supervisor who rewrites that request before anyone moves: "only fetch Rajesh's records, and only the amount column." The supervisor first checks the request makes sense and the columns exist, then applies known efficiency rules, then decides the fastest physical way to do it, and even hands the clerk a pre-printed streamlined worksheet instead of loose instructions. The result arrives far faster, and the person who wrote the request did not have to think about any of it.

**One line to remember:** Catalyst turns a DataFrame or SQL query into an efficient plan through parse, analyze, optimize, and physical planning, cutting data read via predicate pushdown and column pruning and speeding execution with whole-stage code generation.

sections.s2_technical:
Catalyst works in four main phases, each transforming a tree that represents the query. The first phase produces the parsed logical plan: Spark parses your DataFrame operations or SQL text into a tree of logical operators, but at this stage names are unresolved — it does not yet know whether a column or table actually exists. The second phase is analysis: Catalyst resolves references against the catalog, binding column names to actual columns and table names to actual tables, checking types, and producing the analyzed logical plan. If you referenced a column that does not exist, this is where it fails.

The third phase is logical optimization, which is rule-based and is where the famous wins happen. Catalyst applies a library of transformation rules repeatedly until the plan stops changing. Predicate pushdown moves filters as close to the data source as possible, so a filter on account id is pushed into the Parquet or JDBC scan and far less data is read in the first place. Column pruning removes columns the query never uses, so if you only need the amount column Spark does not read the other twenty columns from a columnar file. Other rules include constant folding, combining adjacent filters, and simplifying boolean expressions. The output is the optimized logical plan, which is logically equivalent to the original but much cheaper.

The fourth phase is physical planning. Catalyst takes the optimized logical plan and generates one or more physical plans, choosing concrete strategies — for example, deciding whether a join should be a broadcast hash join or a sort-merge join based on estimated sizes. It uses a cost model to pick the cheapest physical plan. Then, for many operators, it applies whole-stage code generation, which fuses a chain of operators in a stage into a single compiled Java function so the data is processed in tight loops over the JVM rather than through many virtual method calls, dramatically reducing per-row overhead.

A senior nuance is that Catalyst is why DataFrames and SQL usually outperform hand-written RDD code: because you express what you want declaratively, Catalyst sees the whole query and can apply pushdown, pruning, join selection, and codegen, whereas with raw RDDs you must optimize by hand and Spark cannot see inside your lambdas. Catalyst is also extensible — you can add custom rules — and it is complemented at runtime by Adaptive Query Execution, which adjusts the physical plan using actual statistics gathered during execution. In the bank, simply moving legacy RDD jobs to DataFrames let Catalyst push filters into our Parquet reads and prune columns, cutting both input-output and runtime substantially with no manual tuning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A naive query reads every transaction and every column, then filters in memory. This is exactly what predicate pushdown and column pruning fix by reading less at the source.

Problem 2 — Column names in a query might be wrong, and the system must catch that before running. This is exactly the analysis phase resolving references.

Problem 3 — Executing operators one row at a time through many method calls is slow. This is exactly what whole-stage code generation improves by fusing operators.

The mini-project models a tiny Catalyst-style pipeline in Java. A `LogicalPlan` tree is parsed from a request, an `Analyzer` resolves column names against a schema, an `Optimizer` applies predicate pushdown and column pruning rules, and a `PhysicalPlanner` reports a fused codegen stage. The demo issues a request for Rajesh's transaction amounts over a wide schema and shows how many rows and columns are actually read before and after optimization.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions with four columns each — account id, amount, branch, and channel. The query wants only the amount column, and only for Rajesh (SAV2001).

Step 1: The parsed logical plan is built from the request — scan the transactions table, filter where account equals SAV2001, project the amount column. Names are not yet verified.

Step 2: The analyzer resolves the requested column against the schema. The amount column exists, so analysis passes; had the query asked for a nonexistent column, this phase would have failed with a clear error.

Step 3: The optimizer applies two rules. Predicate pushdown marks the account filter to be applied at the scan, and column pruning marks that only the amount column should be read instead of all four.

Step 4: The physical planner reports that scan, filter, and project are fused into one whole-stage-codegen loop. During execution, the pushed-down predicate causes the scan to skip Priya's two rows entirely, so only Rajesh's two rows are read, and only one of the four columns is read.

Step 5: The result is the list of Rajesh's amounts, Rs.1000 and Rs.3000. The logs show rows read as two of four and columns read as one of four — the concrete savings from pushdown and pruning.

Step 6: The journey demonstrates that Catalyst turned a request that would naively read four rows and four columns into one that reads only two rows and one column, with operators fused for speed, all without the author changing the query.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] ANALYZE: resolving column names against schema
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] RULE predicate pushdown: filter account=SAV2001 pushed into scan
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] RULE column pruning: read only [amount]
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] PHYSICAL: whole-stage codegen fuses scan+filter+project into one loop
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] EXECUTE: rows read=2 (of 4), columns read=1 (of 4)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Rajesh amounts = [1000, 3000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Query: SELECT amount FROM transactions WHERE accountId='SAV2001'
    │
    ▼  PARSE
  Parsed Logical Plan:  Project[amount] ← Filter[acct=SAV2001] ← Scan[transactions]
    │
    ▼  ANALYZE (resolve names vs schema: accountId, amount, branch, channel)
  Analyzed Logical Plan  (columns verified)
    │
    ▼  OPTIMIZE (rule-based)
  Optimized: Scan[transactions, cols={amount}, filter acct=SAV2001]
             ├─ predicate pushdown → skip Priya rows at source
             └─ column pruning     → read only 'amount' (1 of 4 cols)
    │
    ▼  PHYSICAL PLAN + WholeStageCodegen (scan+filter+project fused)
  EXECUTE → rows read 2/4, cols read 1/4 → [1000, 3000]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Catalyst Optimizer is Spark SQL's query optimizer, and it is the main reason DataFrames and SQL usually outperform hand-written RDD code. It works in four phases, each transforming a tree that represents the query. First it parses the DataFrame operations or SQL text into a parsed logical plan, where names are not yet resolved. Then it analyzes that plan, resolving column and table names against the catalog, checking types, and failing early if you referenced something that does not exist, which produces the analyzed logical plan.

The third phase is rule-based logical optimization, and this is where the biggest wins come from. Catalyst applies a library of rules repeatedly until the plan stabilizes. Predicate pushdown moves filters as close to the data source as possible, so a filter on account id is pushed into the Parquet or JDBC scan and far less data is read in the first place. Column pruning drops columns the query never uses, so reading only the amount column from a wide columnar file skips all the others. The fourth phase is physical planning, where Catalyst generates physical plans, uses a cost model to choose strategies like broadcast versus sort-merge joins, and applies whole-stage code generation to fuse a chain of operators into a single compiled Java function that processes rows in tight loops instead of through many virtual calls.

In my project at the National Bank of India the practical impact was concrete. When we migrated legacy RDD jobs to DataFrames, Catalyst automatically pushed our account filters into the Parquet reads and pruned the columns we did not need, so our scans read a fraction of the data and runtimes dropped substantially with no manual tuning. The lesson I took away, and the thing I say in interviews, is that by expressing queries declaratively you let Catalyst see the whole plan and optimize it, whereas with raw RDDs Spark cannot look inside your lambdas and you must optimize everything by hand. I also note that Catalyst is complemented at runtime by Adaptive Query Execution, which refines the physical plan using actual statistics gathered while the job runs.
